structure.title: Independent investigations
structure.text: Thirteen essays take up problems across physics. They can be entered separately; contributor notes establish who is making each case.

structure.title: Overlapping foundations
structure.text: Gravity, quantum theory, time, locality, probability, and realism recur across different proposals rather than forming one settled textbook sequence.

people.name: Quantum theory
people.text: Physics' most successful theory of matter and light, whose strangeness the contributors argue about: what does its mathematics say actually exists?

people.name: General relativity
people.text: Einstein's theory that gravity is the curvature of spacetime, set against quantum theory as the second pillar that physics has not yet unified.

people.name: Interpretation
people.text: The question of what a theory that works is really telling us about the world, which these essays treat as a live problem rather than as philosophy.

context.title: Success and disagreement
context.text: Accurate predictions can coexist with disputes about explanation and ontology. The essays take positions within those disputes.
context.takeaway: Distinguish a contributor's proposal from consensus.

passages.quote: they resist unification into a single, comprehensive framework.

context.title: Different entry demands
context.text: Essays vary in technical vocabulary and assumed knowledge. A difficulty in one does not establish that the whole collection is inaccessible.
context.takeaway: Choose an essay by its question.

notice.text: Follow proposed tests and distinguishing evidence.
notice.why: They show how competing accounts could meet physical inquiry.

notice.text: Notice definitions of locality and probability.
notice.why: Familiar words carry precise and contested meanings.

opening: Physics can predict an experiment exquisitely while leaving physicists arguing about what exists. The contributors to this collection take those arguments seriously: how quantum theory relates to gravity, what probability means, and whether apparently distant events require mysterious connections. These are researchers explaining problems they work on, including proposals that remain open to dispute. Reading across the essays brings the unsettled foundations into view, where getting the calculations right does not remove the need to say what kind of world could produce them.
